newsitem.title: USA: Senator sees hope for U.S. capital gains tax cut.
newsitem.headline: Senator sees hope for U.S. capital gains tax cut.

text.p: The White House and Republicans in Congress were starting talks on a capital gains tax cut from points far apart, but a senior senator said Wednesday he was hopeful a compromise could be reached.

"I'm hopeful that when we get down to the nitty gritty everybody will be open and we'll have a real opportunity of working out concessions on both sides," said Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican.
Roth will be part of a bipartisan working group on taxes announced after President Clinton met with congressional leaders earlier this week.
The other two members of the working group will be House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Republican from Texas, and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.

The Clinton administration was starting from a position that capital gains tax relief should be for homes. Taxpayers would be able to exclude up to $250,000 of capital gain realised on the sale of their home, $500,000 if married and filing a joint return. This would replace the current tax-free rollover of gains into a more expensive home.

Republican leaders in Congress want a broad-based capital gains tax cut, not just for homes, which would lower the top rate by at least half to 19 percent. Senate Democrats have proposed a targeted capital gains tax cut for a list of specific areas including small business owners and farmers.
The tax working group will start meeting some time after next week, when the Senate is in recess, Roth said in an interview with a small group of reporters.

Archer, head of the House tax-writing committee, said the administration appeared to have softened its stance somewhat on capital gains tax relief compared with prior years, and that a broad-based cut would be needed to pass Congress.

"If you look at the body language and you look at the words that they're (administration) using, they're saying 'We're open, we're willing to discuss,'" Archer said. "In the end I think they understand that we're not going to be able to pass a bill through this Congress unless it has broad-based capital gains relief," he said.
Roth said he was "encouraged" that Clinton's proposal allowed a $500,000 tax deduction for homes.

"To me it raised the additional question if you're going to give it to the person who has put their savings in their home, what about the family who rents and put their money in investment, should they be treated differently?" Roth said. "My answer is that you ought to treat them all the same."

Rubin at a Senate Finance Committee hearing earlier Wednesday said: "We looked very carefully at the scarce resources we felt were available for tax relief ... I think we've made the right judgments."
In another development showing Democratic movement on capital gains, the second-ranking Senate Democrat offered a plan for deep cuts in the tax on gains based on how long the investment was held.

Sen. Wendell Ford of Kentucky suggested assets held for more than one year be taxed at 28 percent. The rate would fall by two percentage points for each additional year to 14 percent on those held more than eight years.
